and injuries.

tection is available which will 
permit you to discharge your 
moral obligation and protect 
you against loss from claims

alleged negligence.

phase of your insurance pro¬

Liability Insurance.

Canadian Camping 





Towards a Philosophy 

of Cttmpiny 

John Hoyle 

Director: Camp Gay Venture 


There may be those who will question 
whether a philosophy of camping 
exists, and there may be others who 
question the value of attempting to 
formulate such a philosophy. However, 
if one steals a moment to study the 
meaning of the word in common usage, 
the attempt would appear to be justi¬ 
fied. Webster gives us one of the 
definitions: 

“The body of principles underlying 
... a human activity”, while the 
Oxford Dictionary suggests “A 
study of principles of human action 
or conduct”. 

With such definitions surely we, who 
are responsible for the lives of campers 
for an extended period each summer 
should clarify our thinking so that our 
philosophy may be based upon authen¬ 
tic principles, which have been satisfac¬ 
torily integrated, and arc readily ap- 
licable to young life of today. Dr. Karl 
Bernhardt, speaking recently at a meet¬ 
ing of the Ontario Camping Associa¬ 
tion, referring to camping said, “You 
must have a philosophy”. With such 
an authority behind us, we feel safe in 
pursuing our course. 

The following thoughts are, of course, 
not original. They owe their genesis 
to the great Canadian, American, Eng¬ 
lish and European philosophers and 
psychologists of the past and present 
who have studied carefully human na¬ 
ture. They have laid a sound founda¬ 


tion. It is left to us to interpret their 
profound contribution in terms of Can¬ 
adian camping in 1952. 

Let us commence with the most im¬ 
portant person in camp, the camper. 
What is he in reality when you get 
behind the familiar personality? May 
we suggest that he is a human spirit en¬ 
dowed by nature with certain strong 
tendencies pertaining largely to the 
functions of self-protection, survival and 
the will to live. He comes into human 
society not moral or immoral but 
amoral. Certainly he may be pre-dis- 
posed in certain directions but to a very 
great extent, his future is in his own 
hands. 

R. L. Sharpe sums this up so effec¬ 
tively in his poem: 

Each is given a bag of tools, 

A shapeless mass, 

A book of rules; 

And each must make— 

Ere life is flown— 

A stumbling block 
Or a stepping stone. 

By the time the child reaches camp 
he has been already influenced deeply 
by his home, school, church or syna¬ 
gogue, and his entire social environ¬ 
ment. However, he is still “in the mak¬ 
ing”, comparatively easily guided, 
stimulated, and influenced by those 
sensitizing media that emerge and are 
clarified in the freedom of a democratic 
camp situation. 


Toronto, Canada, April , 1952 


7 


Every child has numerous needs, 
some superficial, some which require 
die skilled hand to discover, if he is to 
reach out and reach up to a well- 
balanced life. Obviously a brief article 
such as this cannot attempt to discuss 
these in detail. Many of a child’s 
needs'* may be found within the bounds 
of the following four general classifi¬ 
cations. 

A Realization of Security. The study 
of human nature shows that one of the 
most fundamental needs of both child¬ 
hood and adulthood is a satisfying sense 
of security. This seems basic to any 
well-balanced life at every age level. 
The search for security may be below 
the level of conscious thought in some 
instances but the urge is there, inherent 
in every normal human being. Youth, 
despite his apparent egotism and self- 
sufficiency, undoubtedly feels unstable 
when left completely to his own devices. 
While he craves experience and de¬ 
mands complete liberty he nevertheless 
seeks for the security that he looks back 
to, the security that originated in com¬ 
plete dependence upon mother, father 
and home. Right here is one of the 
conflicts of youth, the conflict between 
the urge to be free, dominant, self-suf¬ 
ficient, and the desire for security and 
dependence. 

New Experience. Youth is restless, 
youth is adventurous, youth is dissatis¬ 
fied with things as they are; the youth 
is scornful of the “status quo”. He 
must have new experiences for his ade¬ 
quate self-completion. In this incessant 
and dominant desire for new experi¬ 
ences lies one of the camp’s greatest 
opportunities, for camp may help child¬ 


ren and youth meet the urge for these 
new experiences constructively on the 
highest level in a controllable environ¬ 
ment. 

Recognition. The developing self of 
the child or youth demands recognition, 
recognition of himself as a person, a 
person apart from others, even those he 
loves and respects. He wants to be of 
value, to experience a sense of achieve¬ 
ment, to be important; with these 
claims go an overpowering desire to 
love and be loved. The child’s stability 
depends very largely on the emotional 
satisfaction he receives from being “ac¬ 
cepted” by his peers—in camp, his 
cabin group. 

A Power outside of Himself. The 
craving for a satisfying inner response 
to a Power outside of himself seems to 
be inherent in human nature. A well- 
balanced personality is greatly depen¬ 
dent on a developing understanding oi 
a growing religious experience adequate 
to his expanding mental, emotional and 
social life. Once again, surely the camp 
is in a strategic position through en¬ 
vironment, leadership, programme and 
atmosphere to reveal to the child the 
permanent values of a healthy personal 
and social religious experience. Despite 
all the well-intentioned endeavours of 
home, church and school, we are fail¬ 
ing to meet adequately this vital and 
very fundamental human urge. It is 
one of the most difficult urges to meet, 
but just because it does present so many 
difficulties, let us not pass it by; let us 
rather accept the challenge and give to 
the problem the best that we have to 
give. 


*—Much of the foregoing material on 
“Needs” is taken from the author’s book 
“Towards the Understanding of Youth”, 
published by the Canadian Council of 
Churches, and used by permission. 


8 


Canadian Camping 



We may summarize what we have 
said as follows. Children and youth 
with certain driving urges must be 
guided aright or they will lead to dis¬ 
aster. How can we attempt to meet 
them? Does not this challenge suggest 
that our camp programme needs to be 
flexible, adventurous, free, and above 
all, purposeful? Purposeful in the sense 
that camp is not a place solely for physi¬ 
cal recreation, but is rather an experi¬ 
ence in effective social living and 
through which children may have the 
happy opportunity, under the guidance 
of understanding and trained leader¬ 
ship, to respond in a constructive way 
to their inner urges. Urges which, if 
skilfully guided, make for happy, well- 
balanced personalities; urges which, if 
left to chance development, will probab¬ 
ly lead to failure and unhappiness. 

To secure an understanding of the 
needs of children in general is not so 
difficult, thanks to the vast amount of 
research already carried out in this 
field, in no place more thoroughly than 
in our own Canada through the twenty- 
five years of tireless effort by the 
faculty of the Institute for Child Study 
in the University of Toronto* and 
other similar centres. However, to 


understand the needs of each individual 
child is quite another question, and far 
too broad a subject to be attempted 
here. Nevertheless, it may be said that 
only to the extent that we as camp 
directors and counsellors are able to 
discern at least some of the specific 
needs of each child in our care, may 
we expect to achieve any lasting mea¬ 
sure of success. Every child is different; 
there is no “average” child to guide us. 
Somehow, ways must be found by 
which at least the major needs of each 
child may be brought to the surface 
and all the skill of the camp leadership 
focussed in that direction. It would 
seem that there are times when the 
child should be encouraged to become 
aware of those needs and his co-opera¬ 
tion sought in meeting them. In other 
cases such an approach would end in 
disaster and such assistance as we may 
be able to give must be subtle and un¬ 
realized by the camper. 

In this article I have presented the 
problem but not the cure. That must 
be left to those life-long students of 
behaviour who are always so willing to 
share with us from the well of their 
experience. 


*—The reader who is interested in the 
scientific aspects of these ideas might see 
Twenty-five Years of Child Study: by the 
staff of the Institute of Child Study, Univer¬ 
sity of Toronto Press; 184 pages; $4.00. 



9 


Toronto , Canada, April , 1952 





Counsellor Meetinys * 

Adele Statten Ebbs 
Director: Camp Wapomeo 


It has often been said that a camp is 
only as good as the staff which it em¬ 
ploys. Of course this statement takes for 
granted that all camp directors or head 
counsellors have the same ability to 
train and co-ordinate their staffs. And 
it is true from the campers’ point of 
view that the success of a camping sea¬ 
son depends on the counsellors. These 
reasons are proof enough that there 
should be opportunities made for staff* 
training during the camp period. This 
“in service” training may be a review 
of a previous course, or in some cases 
the only training which is offered. 

The objectives of staff training are 
similar to that of the camp as a whole. 
From the staff emerges the “camp 
spirit”, holiday atmosphere and eager¬ 
ness for activity. The staff can demon¬ 
strate the democratic way of living in 
a community. The training will demon¬ 
strate the practical application of group 
methods, as well as give insight into the 
needs of individual campers. Finally, 
many program directives will be given, 
some of which we shall develop later. 

There are various ways of training 
staff—all of which should be used. It 
starts with the initial interview during 
the winter, followed up by letters, con¬ 
versations and a few meetings. Pre- 
camp is the ideal training ground. At 


that time everyone is focussed on the 
one job at hand—that of becoming an 
effective camp staff member. When the 
campers arrive in camp, there is comp¬ 
aratively little opportunity for training. 
However, the success must continue in 
various ways. There can be personal 
interviews, plenty of on-the-spot super¬ 
vision (by that I mean observation fol¬ 
lowed by conferences), and lastly the 
so-called Counsellor or Staff meeting. 

Meetings called during the busy days 
of camp must have real value. They 
must be informative and to the point. 
Those attending must be the personnel 
really concerned with the subject at 
hand. If at pre-camp all the main basic 
training has been covered, then the in¬ 
camp meetings will be mostly a review. 
They will give an opportunity to 
demonstrate the general principles in 
practical application. There will be 
general staff meetings of two types: 

(a) A daily review of the day’s pro¬ 
gram and routme announcements. 

(b) A longer session for instruction of 
a more general nature, followed 
by discussion and evaluation. 

(A) At the Daily Meeting all routine 
matters pertaining to the whole staff 
are highlighted. A brief review of the 

* Reprinted by permission from the 
Y.W.C.A. Programme Folder. 


10 


Canadian Camping 


day’s program is given with opportunity 
for synchronizing every department. 
Various departments report. The 
Waterfront Director may check on life¬ 
guards for that day, or may announce 
a regatta, asking for the co-operation 
and participation of most of the camp. 
The Dramatic Department may seek 
assitance in some forthcoming project. 
The Dietitian may have something to 
say (or you may have something to 
say to her). On a scorching hot day, 
the nurse can warn against sunburn. A 
recent campwide event can be briefly 
evaluated, or a committee appointed to 
investigate some problem, or to plan a 
function bringing a report back to the 
meeting a day or so later. A standing 
committee of counsellors elected to 
function over a period can handle 
many problems on policy and routine, 
and bring recommendations to this 
meeting. This gives an idea of the 
diversity of the problems that might 
arise. They should be pertinent to the 
whole camp. Matters concerning only 
a few should be dropped and discussed 
later by those concerned. 

“Gamp Routines” mimeographed, or 
in a notebook, save a lot of valuable 
time, and can be definite about the 
things over which there can be little 
difference of opinion. These include 
Fire Precautions, Fire Drill. Meal 
Hours, Tuck Shop, Mail, Food Parcels, 
Cash, Days Off, Sunday Suppers (Pic¬ 
nics), Care of Equipment, Laundry, 
Transportation schedules, Lost and 
Found, Officer of the Day and Night 
Watch schedules. 

A “Staff Organization chart” gives 
guidance to all. The names of the com¬ 
plete staff are included: Counselling, 
Kitchen and Maintenance. If this is 
given out at the beginning of the camp 
it helps to get everyone acquainted, 
and to familiarize the new staff with 
the structure of the organization. 


(B) General Staff Meetings will be held 
less frequently because of the time in¬ 
volved. It is obvious that during camp 
there is never a meeting at which 
everyone can be present, so the time 
chosen will depend on the individual 
camp. If no pre-camp training has 
been possible, then these topics should 
be introduced as early as possible in the 
season. To decide on the order of their 
presentation is a problem, because all 
are of vital importance. 

1. Health and Safety —The staff it¬ 
self immediately upon arrival in camp 
must be impressed with the necessity of 
taking every precaution to guard their 
campers’ as well as their own health. 
Simple and clear instructions should be 
given on health routine: daily inspec¬ 
tion, sleep, rest and cleanliness. Pro¬ 
cedures should be discussed to prevent 
sunburn, fatigue, accident from fire, use 
of axes, etc., and routines on the water¬ 
front should be set up. Various staff 
members particularly concerned should 
be prepared to discuss the various as¬ 
pects of camp health and safety—the 
doctor or nurse, the dietitian, the camp 
craft and tripping counsellors, the 
water-front director and so on. A very 
careful briefing must be made regard¬ 
ing the first day of camp. All staff 
members should be alerted to their 
specific responsibilities which start the 
moment the first camper comes under 
camp supervision. 

2. The Role of Camping —This topic 
would give a background to the whole 
business of camping, how and where it 
started; how it has developed through 
the years; where it is heading in the 
future; what it claims to do for the 
campers. This makes the counsellors 
realize that they are a part of a large 
and vital organization on this continent 
today. The Canadian and American 
Camping Associations are becoming 
stronger as people realize what and who 


Toronto , Canada , April , 1952 


they represent. These Associations have 
set high standards for themselves, not 
through pressure, but because they are 
composed of a group of people with 
high personal standards. The aims and 
objectives of the individual camp would 
come into this discussion, and to be 
more specific each counsellor should 
have her own objectives and be sensi¬ 
tive to those of her campers and their 
parents. 

3. Program Planning —Keep in sight 
the campers’ point of view. They are 
going to camp this summer primarily 
to have fun. It is a holiday—a glorious 
experience away from home and school 
—not only freedom from routine, but 
freedom to explore the realms of friend¬ 
ship and human relations, 

Let us analyze a 24-hour day at 
camp. Nine or ten hours of sleep; three 
meals a day takes about four hours; a 
rest period lasts one hour at least; an¬ 
other three hours for routine, such as 
getting up, flag raising, clean-up, Hag 
lowering and getting to bed. This all 
adds up to twenty hours, leaving four 
hours for all the other camp activities. 
And during this four hours is the only 
chance to find some leisure—some time 
to just sit in the sun and loaf. It is very 
important that during this time our 
campers should have a positive feeling 
of being able to plan it for therm-elves. 
All the rest of the year these children’s 
standards are set by adults. Some 
homes are quite democratic, but it is 
very hard to find any set of parents 
who can keep themselves in the back¬ 
ground. At school the children have 
practically no say in what they are 
going to learn—or even how they may 
go about it. Camp is the only com¬ 
munity which is run entirely for chil¬ 
dren with the sole purpose of fulfilling 
their needs. Let’s keep it that way. 


Primarily the camp-site itself largely 
determines what activities are going to 
exist and what are going to predomi¬ 
nate. There is usually water enough 
for swimming—but the type and extent 
of the water-craft will differ. So here 
are two factors that have much to do 
with program planning—(1) the camp¬ 
site and equipment and (2) the aims 
and objectives of specific camps. 

The two other directives in program 
planning are more under our control— 
the counsellors and the campers them¬ 
selves. The director need not feel that 
she will be handling the program for 
the campers all by herself; the resources 
of the entire staff should be pooled. 
Campers enjoy having the opportunity 
of getting to know other members of 
the staff—a change is as good as a rest. 
As for the campers’ part in program¬ 
planning, this is the whole secret of a 
happy and satisfying summer for them. 
We do a lot of talking about the demo¬ 
cratic way of life—of being good citi¬ 
zens in a democracy, and so on. One 
cannot live that life or be a good citi¬ 
zen unless one practises it from an early 
age. At camp we can give the campers 
this opportunity. In order to develop in 
responsibility, independence and ability 
to make wise decisions, we must provide 
varied opportunities for choice. 

In early days of camp, the counsel¬ 
lor’s job was relatively simple. The 
range of activities and resources were 
limited. If there was a champion diver 
or swimmer on the staff—fine; the 
campers surely would learn to swim 
and dive—or else. An Indian in charge 
of canoeing would teach the paddling. 
That is all right up to a point—if you 
can have a champion who also has the 
personality to teach young children and 
who understands their individual dif¬ 
ferences, their abilities, their fears, their 


12 


Canadian Camping 


emotional development. But to find 
one with the patience, understanding 
and the insight of a trained psychologist 
is difficult. Most activities at one time 
were motivated by the children them¬ 
selves seeking awards. Individual com¬ 
petition dominated the day. Today 
many people do not believe that is the 
best way to get campers to participate 
in activities. But sometimes there is 
such a strong feeling of expectancy that 
everyone will participate in all activi¬ 
ties, that it virtually amounts to com¬ 
pulsory participation. With all these 
external means of motivation there 
would be little opportunity for the chil¬ 
dren themselves to exercise the power of 
making their own decisions. So the 
potentialities for developing into strong, 
thoughtful and positive individuals 
would be lost. 

4. The Cabin Group —Since this group 
exerts the greatest influence on the indi¬ 
vidual camper, it is important that the 
counsellor be skillful in the art of group 
leadership. The campers should be al¬ 
lowed to choose their cabin mates 
whenever possible. The first few days 
are very important. It may be necessary 
for the counsellor to guide the group 
skillfully, suggesting projects and enter¬ 
prises which will knit the group to¬ 
gether. Each individual must develop 
a feeling of belonging which can be in¬ 
creased by responsibility being given in 
tasks and decision making. There 
should be a feeling of “give and take”. 
The group experiences should be so 
varied that the same camper is not 
always the leader. Look for opportuni¬ 
ties to bring forward the one who shuns 
the limelight. For the staff meeting one 
counsellor might be prepared to lead 
a discussion using a specific example to 
illustrate the development of this pro¬ 
cess of “give and take”. Experi¬ 
enced leaders could reconstruct the situ¬ 
ation into a socio-drama. 


5. Spiritual Values —The following is 
developed from the notes of a presen¬ 
tation at a pre-camp course in July, 
1950. There are various approaches to 
the appreciation of nature—that of an 
artist, a naturalist or a geologist. A 
counsellor must make sure that the 
campers, especially the sensitive camp¬ 
ers, have opportunity for quiet commu¬ 
nion.. At dawn and dusk this feeling 
or need should have the chance of ex¬ 
pression. In evening discussions around 
the campfire or at bedtime, there should 
be opportunity for quiet talk. Toler¬ 
ance can be developed. There should 
be a feeling of freedom of expression 
and sympathetic understanding. At 
morning meditations another opportu¬ 
nity is given for quiet thought. Some¬ 
times it may be directed or stimulated 
by a leader, other times guided only by 
the strains of quiet music. There are 
camp institutions such as Council Ring 
and Chapel services which create a re¬ 
ceptive atmosphere. The democratic 
way of life has been mentioned before. 
Where can it fetter understood and 
expressed than at camp. 

The topics discussed above are sug¬ 
gestions to be included in counsellor 
meetings during camp (or in pre¬ 
camp) . These may be given to the 
whole staff, or to unit meetings acord- 
ing to the age groups with whom the 
staff is concerned. It seems satisfactory 
to present the topics to the group as a 
whole, and after to have the counsellors 
divide into unit groups for more specific 
discussion. 

Counsellor Meetings can be fun. It 
is a time when the adult group in camp 
can get together and talk in their own 
language. It is extremely valuable for 
building up morale, and reassuring 
every member of the staff that she has 
an important role to play. In finishing, 
may I quote from a letter written by 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1952 


13 


Taylor Statten to his stafl': “The satis¬ 
faction that a conscientious counsellor 
gets out of working with children is 
very great, and as a result of the experi¬ 
ence and training one should gain some 
understanding of child psychology and 
group methods which we hope will 
contribute toward a more skillful and 
intelligent parenthood.’ 5

Nature iiuidinii 

William G. Vinal 


One of the outstanding leaders at 
last year’s Quebec Camping Associa¬ 
tion Conference in Montreal was 
“Cap’n Bill” Vinal, Professor of Nature 
Education, University of Massachusetts. 
Dr. Vinal is the author of one of the 
most indispensable nature books for 
camp leaders— “Nature Guiding He 
has also published many inexpensive 
pamphlets of great practical value to 
counsellors. Those who were fortunate 
enough to be present at his “Nature 
Seminar” last spring, were intrigued 
with his lively and stimulating com¬ 
ments, his vast fund of knowledge and 
his skillful and often amusing handling 
of questions. Some of the questions 
and answers are given below: 

How would you start a class of begin¬ 
ners in Nature Study? 

First of all, it is not a class, and it 
should not be a study. I would avoid 
school vocabulary, which unfortunately 
gives it a stigma. Give them something 
with adventure or a challenge. Offer 
many different opportunities. Let the 
group choose. For instance, you might 
get an old lumber man to guide them in 
constructing a cabin. 

How can we correlate craft work to 
the subject of nature? 

Better forget “correlate and subject”. 
Do things! Tin can cookery is nature 
too. Let them make the tin-can stove; 
let them find out about the various 
kinds of fires and wood to use. 


What do you think are the most im¬ 
portant things in a camp musem? 

Campers! It should be a campers’ 
museum—tempory, rather than perma¬ 
nent. A workshop, rather than a store¬ 
house, and it should be strictly local. 

Why do you suggest workshops? 

It is doing that puts life into any pro¬ 
ject. Making leaf prints, or casts of 
foot prints or bark baskets is a better 
investment of time than just gazing 
at someone’s collection of mounted 
leaves or a stuffed chipmunk. 

What type of museum would you 
build? 

The camp grounds is a museum. 
Have the campers build a rock garden, 
or an over-night shelter or a nature 
trail. If you must build something, 
make it a workshop. 

Is it worthwhile to make a nature 
trail and label everything with tags? 

Yes, if the campers do it! No, if it is 
made for them by the counsellors! The 
value is in the making. It can be a 
very valuable experience for every one 
taking part in it. 

What would say about a counsellor 
who insists on using a scientific 
vocabulary? 

If you mean the Latin names for 
everything, I would be tempted to ask 
him to speak English! 


Toronto, Canada , April, 1952 


15 


Do you think that badges and awards 
are stimulating? 

Yes, but it is the wrong stimulus. 
Campers are then working for badges 
and not for the fun of the experience. 
When they collect thirty tree speci¬ 
mens, they are through. 

What do you think about a director 
who says that children should not stay 
up to study stars? 

Directors need to be educated tool 
City children scarcely ever have an op¬ 
portunity to even see a star! All they 
know about them is: “Twinkle, 

twinkle, little star, how I wonder what 
you are.” A night hike on a camp¬ 
ing-out trip is a grand opportunity for 
star study. Campers should also have 
the thrill of paddling up the pathway of 
the moon. 


How do you get natural-born nature 
counsellors on your staff? 

They aren’t just born, they’re trained. 
That’s why we have training courses 
and no end of books, nature magazines 
and pamphlets. But even so, good 
nature counsellors are few and precious. 
If you wish counsellors to promote 
outdoor knowledge at camp, be sure 
they have the interest and enthusiasm 
and a degree of knowledge before they 
come. Do not schedule nature at the 
same time as athletics. A pre-camp 
training period for counsellors might be 
useful. Nature leadership requires prac¬ 
tice and imagination. The Scouts often 
make reports in assembly on “What I 
Saw”. Children see many things and 
make fine reports if given the chance. 
A successful season means a succession 
of successful happenings. 



16

Canadian Campinff 
News Letter 

Dear Camping Friends: 

As you will read elsewhere in this 
issue of the Canadian Camping, the 
Association recently held its annual 
meeting and a number of us have as¬ 
sumed the responsibility of carrying on 
as your officers for the coming year. 

In the past few years those people 
responsible for carrying the work of the 
association have made a significant con¬ 
tribution. Probably the most important 
step forward was the obtaining of our 
Charter as a National Organization of 
camping people in Canada. 

As we see it, the main fuction of our 
C.C.A. is to strengthen, wherever 
possible, the work of Provincial Associa¬ 
tions; since in any country as wide¬ 
spread as our Dominion of Canada, it 
seems logical that the most helpful 
service to individual camp people will 
come through the work ol organized 
groups right in their own area. Each 
of these local Camping Associations is 
dedicated to the development and 
maintainance of high camping stan¬ 
dards and to the study and appreciation 
of wider aspects of the movement. 
Members believe that through discus¬ 
sion and consideration of camping poli¬ 
cies and problems and by the exchange 
of ideas and information, better camp¬ 
ing will be achieved. 

Sometimes there are opportunities for 
our camping people from wide-spread 
points across the country to meet face to 
face, but more often than not the mem¬ 
bers of the C.C.A. know one another 
and benefit from the services of their 
association through the mail. It is our 
sincere hope that members will write 
to the new office at 52 Avenue Road, 
Toronto, more frequently than ever 


and also that they will be sure to cor¬ 
respond directly with the Chairman of 
various standing committees who are 
anxious to assist them with their camp 
problems. 

Within the wide frame-work of tying 
together the work of Provincial Associa¬ 
tions and of encouraging the formation 
of new Provincial bodies, your execu¬ 
tive committee sees the following as 
some of its more specific responsibilities. 

(1) To distribute information as a 
National Association and to repres¬ 
ent organized camping at the 
national level whenever required. 

(2) To assist in making information 
developed by Local Associations 
available to all members across 
the country. 

(3) To act as a resource body for Pro¬ 
vincial Associations and individual 
members across the country, 
through the work of active stand¬ 
ing committees. 

(4) To provide, through the Canadian 
Camping Magazine a means for 
telling the story of Canadian 
Camping and for keeping our 
Camp people well informed. 

We have listed below the member¬ 
ship in the Canadian Camping Associa¬ 
tion as reported at the last annual meet¬ 
ing, and it is significant that at this 
meeting the fee paid to the C.C.A. by 
Provincial Associations was reduced to 
$3.50 for camp members and $1.50 for 
bona fide individual members. This 
was a unanimous decision and it grew 
from a concern for further strength¬ 
ening the work of Provincial Associa¬ 
tions. It is our hope that by entering 
into a co-operative arrangement with 
the Ontario Camping Association full¬ 
time office, we will, with the help of the 
executive secretary of that office, be

tiuehee Section 
Animal Conference 

Hedley S. Dimock, Dean of George 
Williams College is to be the key 
speaker at the Quebec Camping As¬ 
sociation Annual Spring Conference, to 
be held in Montreal, April 4th and 5th, 
1952. 

Dr. Dimock is past president of the 
American Camping Association, and co¬ 
author of Camping and Character and 
Administration of the Modern Camp. 
Dr. Dimock will address the opening 
banquet Friday evening on “A Critical 
Look at Modern Camping.” He will 
also lead three discussion groups—1) 
Pre-camp Training, 2) Incamp Super¬ 
vision, and 3) Evaluation. 

Some three hundred camp directors, 
staff and counsellors will attend the 
conference being held at the Sir Arthur 
Currie Memorial Gymnasium Building 
of the McGill University. Featured at 
the Conference will be discussion 
groups, workshops, practical demonstra¬ 
tions, lectures, and display booths ol 
some twenty firms displaying camp 
goods and equipment. 

Walter Meyer, internationally known 
song leader will lead the conference 
singing, as well as three sessons in “Song 
Leading in Camps”. Meyer specializes 
in international folk songs. 

Louis Thomas will give leadership 
to the workshop on Indian Lore and 
crafts. Mr. Thomas is an Iroquois 
Indian and a leading authority on 
Indian Lore in this part of the country. 

By popular demand Dr. Carter Store 
of Ottawa will again lead the camp- 
craft sessions of the Conference. Dr. 
Store is well known in this field. 

Don Rose of the Red Cross and Clair 
Buckley of the Y.M.C.A. will hold forth 
in McGill University’s fine new pool on 
practical sessions in teaching swimming, 
water safety and life saving.

Kanawana is president of the Quebec 
Camping Association. 

Further information on the Confer¬ 
ence is available from either of the

Convention 1952 

The 22nd national biennial conven¬ 
tion ol the American Camping Associa¬ 
tion will be held at the Conrad Hilton 
in Chicago, April 16, 17, 18, 19, 1952. 

Among the groups and organizations 
which will participate in the Conven¬ 
tion ol the American Camping Associa¬ 
tion are: Protestant Camps, Catholic 
Camps, Boys’ Clubs, Boy Scouts, 
Campfire Girls, Girl Scouts, 4-H Ex¬ 
tension Service Camp, Salvation Army, 
Y.M.C.A., Y.W.C.A., Settlement 
Houses, and the private camps. Live 
demonstrations will be given in mass 
food preparation, camp cookouts, cre¬ 
ative arts, handicrafts and conservation. 

An innovation of the 1952 National 
Camping Convention will be the intro¬ 
duction of seminars. Rey Carlson, as¬ 
sociate director of recreation, Univer¬ 
sity of Indiana, and former president 
ol the American Camping Association, 
will lead the seminar on camp admini¬ 
stration. Kit Hammett, camp consultant 
and former secretary of the American 
Camping Association, will lead the 
seminar on camp program. 

Further information about registra¬ 
tion for the Convention can be obtained 
by writing the American Camping Asso¬ 
ciation, 343 S. Dearborn St., Chicago, 
or Joseph N. Clemens, convention 
chairman, 123 W. Madison St., Rm. 
2200, Chicago 2, Illinois. 


Canadian Campinf/ 
Convention 

Jointly Sponsored by the Ontario 
Camping Association. 

A generous amount of back-slapping 
along with higher-than-average praise 
are in order for the committees who 
turned out such good fare for the Cana¬ 
dian Camping Convention. Sponsored 
jointly by the Canadian Camping 
Association and the Ontario Camping 
Association at Central Y.W.C.A. in 
Toronto on February 29th and March 
1st, it was climaxed by the annual 
meeting of the Canadian Camping 
Association at which Ted Yard was 
elected President of C.C.A. for 1952-3. 
It is during this term that C.C.A. office 
is transferred to Toronto. 

In spreading the gospel of camplore 
and campcraft, it cannot be said that 
any one phase of the conference out¬ 
shone another, actually. Each discus¬ 
sion group, kindred group meeting, 
workshop and address held its own ap¬ 
peal; in fact, quite a difficulty arose 
when a choice of sessions presented 
itself to delegates. 

Dr. Carter Storr, guest speaker from 
Ottawa, drew a large audience. Any¬ 
one who has heard him speak on out- 
tripping and its various ramifications 
w'ants to hear him again. His fame 
had spread far and wide by the time he 
reached Toronto, so his audiences were 
large . . . and not disappointed. 

If any one speaker stood out, it 
could be said that Mr. R. E. K. Rourke, 
Headmaster of Pickering College and 
Director of Camp Mazinaw, kept Fri¬ 
day evening’s diners listening and 
laughing at one and the same time. 
With the usual mastery of his subject 
combined with his equally famous mas¬ 
tery of wit, he was able to put across 


Toronto , Canada , April, 1952 


21 


one of the most convincing talks on 
camping, with more than the usual 
amount of punch. 

Dr. Alvin Cooper, Director of Lea¬ 
dership Education for the United 
Church of Canada presented a study of 
Persuasive Camp Programming at Sat¬ 
urday’s luncheon; on the same day, the 
closing address was given by Mr. Wilbur 
Howard, Field Secretary of Christian 
Education, Manitoba Conference, Uni¬ 
ted Church of Canada. He used as 
his topic: The Trail to High Adventure. 

No camp category was left out. 
Every kind of camp was able to parti¬ 
cipate to a greater extent than ever 
before. Agency and Day Camps, Y. 
Camps, Private and Church Camps 
heard their own problems discussed 
under such varied topics as Camp Ex¬ 
penses, Variety in Programme Plan¬ 
ning, Crafts, Waterfront Activities, 
Creative Handicrafts. And speaking of 
handicrafts, Mr. George Clifton from 
Bark Lake C.I.T. Camp took up the 
front of the auditorium with an imagin¬ 
ative display of artwork produced most¬ 
ly with those everyday bits of equipment 
each camper has at his or her fingertips 
all summer long: twigs, cones, burrs, 
driftwood ... to mention a few. 

Mr. David Palter’s films sent every 
counsellor and director home in the 
mood to pack for camp next week and 
the generosity of the exhibitors with 
their lucky draws added a spark of 
excitement to the whole event. 

Congratulations to Mr. C. T. Sharpe, 
Chairman, Mr. Ron Hanagan, Mr. 
John Hoyle (OCA President), Mr. 
William Chapman and Miss Joyce 
Bertram for a project well thought out 
and successfully carried through!

Hook Itevietvs 

The Theory of Camping: An introduc¬ 
tion to Camping in Education, by 
Frank L. Irwin, Ed.D., A. S. Barnes 
and Co., New York; 1950; pp. 178. 

This book, “written primarily for 
camp directors, camp counsellors, pub¬ 
lic school administrators, teachers and 
college students, seeks to present a com¬ 
prehensive view of the educational as¬ 
pects of organized camping, an under¬ 
standing of the part camping can play 
in achieving the goals or aims of Ameri¬ 
can education, and an acquaintance 
with the specific methods by which 
camping can be utilized to achieve 
these goals or aims.” This statement 


demonstrates both the purpose and 
style of the book. 

The content is good. It includes 
chapters on “organized camping in the 
United States. Education in the Twen¬ 
tieth Century. Understanding the 
campers. Group life. The program. 
The counsellor, administration, day 
camping and the public school camp. 
It contains a considerable amount of 
information in the text and in the well 
selected references. 

It should be in a camp library, al¬ 
though its chief function would seem to 
be that ol a text book for camp courses. 
The material although solid, is a little 
dull and it is a pity that it loses its 
clarity by being set in too small type.

Canadians of Long Ago: The Story of 
the Canadian Indian, by Kenneth E. 
Kidd, Royal Ontario Museum; Long¬ 
mans, Green and Co., 1951; pp. 174; 
price, $2.25 (Illustrations by Sylvia 
Hahn). 

Many camps use council rings and 
other customs which campers often 
erroneously accept as being typical of 
real Indian life. While the fun and 
zest of the “Council Ring” forms an 
exciting part of camp life, most child¬ 
ren would find the real things Indians 
did and created even more fascinating. 
Mr. Kidd’s book, written for school 
children, is interesting, attractive and 
authentic. 

Miss Hahn’s illustrations of Indian 
homes, tools, canoes, clothes and masks, 
suggest many designs for the arts and 
crafts programme. It includes accounts 
of Indian living, homes, families, hunt¬ 
ing, fishing craft work, festivals, des¬ 
criptions of their customs and beliefs, 
and a short chapter on their heritage 
to us. 

Children of course know that reality 
is more exciting than fantasy; as we 
adults develop this point of view, we 
can at least supplement our pictur¬ 
esque “Indian” ceremonies with an 
understanding of the real life and 
thoughts of the Canadians of Lonv 
Ago.

A Low Cost Toilet for a Short-Term 
Camp. 

Long-term summer camps with per¬ 
manent campsites need adequate well- 
built sanitary facilities.* However, 
many organizations operating camps of 
one or two weeks’ duration on rented 
sites do not find it possible to provide 
such toilets, and need a simple yet 
effective design for a substitute. This 
design might also be used by large 
organized camps operating a canoe trip 
outpost at some distance from the main 
camp. 

A wooden box consisting of two ends, 
two sides and a top but no bottom, 
should be constructed out of one inch 
dressed tongued and grooved lumber, 
or five-eighths inch thick plywood 
made with exterior-type glue. It should 
be about 20” wide by 30” long by 14” 
high. A toilet seat hole with rounded 
edges is cut through the top surface fif¬ 
teen inches from either end and near 
the front side. This hole should not be 
circular, but should be cut to the same 
shape as a standard toilet seat. If 
tongued and grooved boards are used, 
the sides of the hole will have to be 
braced on the inside. A board top 
hinged at the back with two brass hinges 
is provided to cover the hole when not 
in use. The inside of the box must be 
painted with two coats of roofing or 
boat pitch. The outside surface should 
be treated with a wood preservative 
such as creosote, or painted. The box 


26 


Canadian Camping 












can be carried by two people if two 
stretcher-type handles are nailed along 
the sides. 

A hole slightly smaller than the box 
in area, and about two feet deep, is 
dug, over which the box is placed. A 
screen made of burlap, sacking, or old 
tent canvas is erected around the toilet 
by using wooden poles. A useful addi¬ 
tion to the toilet can be made by remov¬ 
ing the top from a small wooden box, 
placing the box on side on a suitable 
support, and hanging a toilet paper 
holder inside it. Space for a container 
of chloride of lime would be useful as 
well. All of this equipment can be 
cleaned and stored away for reuse for 
many camping seasons. 

R. K. Cleverdon, 
Camp Kandalore. 

* See Canadian Camping, December, 1950 


COMBINED OPERATION: 

If you have riding and canoeing at 
your camp this is a form of expedition 
that has a tinge of adventure. You 
could try it too by combining horses and 
hikers, canoeists and sailing groups. We 
called it 

“HORSEANOE” 

The destination of the horses and 
canoes is a rendezvous for lunch or 
dinner, or even an “over-night”. Those 
who ride on the outward trip will pad¬ 
dle home, and vice versa. The choice 
of route and destination, the timing, 
the menu, all call for planning before¬ 
hand. Sometimes the counsellors might 
make the plans and create a mystery 
trip for the campers; in other situations 
the planning is a valuable and enjoy¬ 
able part of the experience for the 
campers themselves—conferring with 
the activity or other counsellors 
concerned.

DICTIONARY OF DISCARDS 

Frank M. Rich 

This A-to-Z checklist gives you more than 
7,000 ideas for making useful things out of 
scrap materials found around home, garage, 
barn, school or camp. 

Handicrafters, recreation leaders, teachers, 
home owners, campers, farmers, and just plain

I he iood may be carried in the 
canoes, or in a wagon or surrey which 
sets out ahead of the riders. Riding 
breeches aren’t comfortable garb for 
paddling; it is better for the riders to 
wear dungarees or slacks. The canoe¬ 
ists might arrange to arrive first at the 
rendez vous in which case they would 
gather wood, start the fire and prepare 
the hot food or drinks. When the riders 
arrive they will need first to attend to 
their horses. You might plan, therefore, 
that the one group prepare the meal 
and the other group clean up; although 
if they co-operate well volunteers from 
both groups may enjoy working to¬ 
gether. Time for a stroll, a sing-song or 
even a “hunt the dessert” game com¬ 
pletes the fun before setting off home— 
with maybe a sunset to top off the day. 

You may be lucky in knowing a 
farmer whose place is the right distance 
from camp with stable room for your 
horses, or a suitable corral, and then 
the “over-night” is posible. While the 
canoes might carry the bedrolls, it may 
be better to despatch them by truck, 
being sure the driver knows exactly 
where to deliver them! Here is a com¬ 
bined operation where good planning 
and co-operation rate high as factors in 
its success. 

Dorothy Douglas

Algonquin Park Nature Trails Pro¬ 
gramme, an Ontario Department of 
Lands and Forests project, has com¬ 
pleted its seventh successful year. Last 
summer, in addition to conducting more 
than four hundred persons on twenty- 
two scheduled Nature Trail Hikes, 
department biologists made sixteen 
visits to Boys’ and Girls’ Camps in the 
Park to give talks on natural history, 
show slides and films and emphasize 
forest fire prevention. 

In 1944, an impromptu, guided, 
nature hike led to others and eventually 
the matter was deemed of sufficient 
importance to be sponsored by the 
Ontario Department of Lands and For¬ 
ests. As soon as a competent biologist 
could be assigned to the project, the 
first permanent nature trail was laid 
out and the representative trees, shrubs 
and plants were labelled for easy identi¬ 
fication by the public. 

In 1946, the first attempt at a Park 
Museum was housed in a tent alongside 
the highway near Cache Lake. So many 
visitors stopped off at this embryo mus¬ 
eum to view the array of native plant 
and wildlife displayed, that Depart¬ 
ment officials decided that a more wor¬ 
thy, permanent structure should contain 
the Algonquin Park Museum of Natural 
History. Plans were drawn for an at¬ 
tractive log-siding, typically “woodsey” 
building which is now under construc¬ 
tion, parts of which will be ready for 
the 1952 season. On display at the mus¬ 
eum will be specimens of the many 
varieties of floral and faunal life that 



30 


Canadian Camping 






abound in the Park as well as exhibits 
to explain its geography. An insect 
collection is being completed. Adding 
to the enjoyment and education of visi¬ 
tors is a pamphlet describing the Park 
and its Nature Trails Programme. 
Other pamphlets in the making will 
describe native features and inhabitants. 

GETTING ACQUAINTED GAMES 
Name Game (All Ages) 

Method: Circle formation. Two 

minutes are given to learn the names 
of the campers on the left and right. 
The camper in the centre of the circle 
points to someone and says “left” or 


“right”. The-one indicated must call 
out the name of her neighbour before 
the camper in the centre counts to 
ten. If she fails, she changes places 
with the one in the centre. 

Thumbnail Sketch (All Ages) 

Method: Each? camper chooses a 
partner. In three minutes they learn 
five things about each other such as: 
What is your name? Where are you 
from? What cabin do you live in? How 
long have you been a camper? What 
is your hobby? 

Each camper then gives a thumbnail 
sketch of the camper she has just met.

Once there was a camper 

Who thought she’d like to cook, 
But when they went out tripping, 
They didn’t take a book. 

She asked a lot of questions 
About her applesauce 
Until her patient leader 
Was really at a loss. 

She cooked it to perfection— 

A simply super brew, 

And then she asked the leader, 

“Now what am I to do?” 


“Why put it, my dear camper, 

Down in the lake to cool.” 

Which she did. 

M.L.N.

through your fields?”

certainly take a short cut!”
